Status: PROVISIONAL AUDITED EDITION — export reconciliation pending. Created 20 November 2026. This is a non-destructive new working edition. The original World Bible and previous Compendium remain available as separate reference pages; selected entries have now been explicitly revised at the creator's direction (including Gloin's age and the Day 19 back-alley opening), so they must no longer be described as untouched archival copies. Nothing not yet supported by the available records is invented or silently promoted to canon. ## Historical urbanism reference — Rome, Londinium and Eryndor's millennia-old cities Creator priority: Real historical urban population sizes do not cap or disprove fantasy populations. In particular, Karak-Varn is 22.8 million in the adopted sixfold census; 3.8 million was the previous baseline, and the seven Khazari Thrones and their other established populations stay intact. Eryndor's societies are often thousands of years old, with extraordinary engineering, infrastructure, magic and technological possibilities that should be allowed to develop on their own terms. Verified comparison: Ancient Rome is often estimated at 750,000–1 million inhabitants during the early Empire, with scholars disagreeing on exact numbers; one alternative scholarly estimate is around 450,000. The London Museum reports around 30,000 in Londinium by 150 CE; other historical estimates run to \~45,000–60,000, not 1 million. The creator's suggestion that a Rome surviving a few more centuries might have developed cities of 2–3 million is an interesting counterfactual, not a historically verified projection. Sources: [Cambridge Economic History, Early Roman Empire: Production](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/cambridge-economic-history-of-the-grecoroman-world/early-roman-empire-production/D3F384EB636F47D422B2AC9EF2551F39); [Cambridge, Migration and the Urban Economy of Rome](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/demography-and-the-graecoroman-world/migration-and-the-urban-economy-of-rome/FD30B46CBF0A846A84E17783E4635993); [Antiquity population-method alternative](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/antiquity/article/the-population-of-ancient-rome/BACD7DF32B0B77609CD6713B8AF88882); [London Museum, Roman London timeline](https://www.londonmuseum.org.uk/collections/london-stories/timeline-roman-london-londinium/). What history should inspire: The deeply interesting questions of how a metropolis sustains itself: food imports and farming, storage, water, sanitation, roads, ports, technical and professional guilds, taxes, housing, entertainment, bureaucracy and political stability. Roman historians show the importance of major trade networks and imported grain for Rome; Eryndor can build equivalents or invent spectacular in-world solutions. Do not turn context into a limitation: A Khazari city of 22.8m can use vast multi-level caverns, engineered Deepways, huge workshops and farms, rune-enabled systems, or other striking fantasy methods, without calculating its way down to a historical population benchmark. A civilization's millennia of history allows richer accumulated technical and social institutions; it does not require linear growth, no setbacks, or a single dynasty staying in power for thousands of years. Historical comparators are texture, never vetoes, and the Rule of Cool remains: ridiculous-looking ideas may work or fail according to the actual setting, not their appearance. ## Wider urban history comparison — Constantinople, Cairo and Chinese capitals Creator's additional examples: The owner correctly raises Constantinople, Cairo and China's enormous historical capitals as further evidence that the premodern world was capable of very large cities. Fantasy population totals are not subject to historical ceiling tests; Karak-Varn's current modeled population is 22.8 million, superseding its earlier 3.8-million baseline. These figures are historical scholarship analogies, not additional Eryndor populations. | Real historical city | Period | Scholarly size estimate / uncertainty | | --- | --- | --- | | Constantinople | Early sixth century; later twelfth century recovery | Often estimated at about 375,000–500,000 in the Justinianic period. Some older estimates rise toward 1 million, but the million figure is not secure; late-twelfth-century studies report at least 400,000 in some estimates. | | Cairo / Fustat | Mamluk and earlier medieval periods | Cambridge scholar Boaz Shoshan gives \~250,000–500,000 by the mid-fourteenth century, with later losses during plague; wider Cairo versus urban core and period affect estimates. One million in medieval Cairo is not reliably established. | | Tang Chang'an | Eighth century | Large premodern Asian metropolis, with some historical reconstructions around 700,000–800,000 or more, depending on whether all surrounding urban residents count; no definitive census. | | Song Kaifeng | Northern Song, roughly 1000–1126 CE | Approximately one million in Columbia University's comparative teaching material; other scholarship offers smaller values, so estimate is disputed rather than an exact fact. | | Song Hangzhou | Southern Song, 1127–1279 CE | Approximately one million in Columbia University's teaching material; other historical reconstructions also suggest around 1.1m, depending on date and district count. | Primary supporting material and scholarly context: - [Columbia University, Asia for Educators: Cities of the Song](https://afe.easia.columbia.edu/songdynasty-module/cities-new.html) — both Kaifeng and Hangzhou around a million, busy street markets, shops, restaurants, multistory houses, fire stations and charitable/public medical facilities. Columbia describes 14 fire stations and 2,000 fire-control soldiers in Kaifeng; precise local division merits source caution. - [Boaz Shoshan, Popular Culture in Medieval Cairo (Cambridge University Press), Introduction](https://assets.cambridge.org/97805214/32092/sample/9780521432092ws.pdf) — estimated Cairo 250k–500k before major plague declines; multistory Fustat dwellings, thousands of sellers, dense social stratification, and caution about travelers' exaggerated numeric comparisons. - [Anthony Kaldellis, Civic Identity and Civic Participation in Constantinople](https://www.academia.edu/80201228/_Civic_Identity_and_Civic_Participation_in_Constantinople_in_C%C3%A9dric_Br%C3%A9laz_and_Els_Rose_eds_Civic_Identity_and_Civic_Participation_in_Late_Antiquity_and_the_Early_Middle_Ages_Turnhout_Brepols_2021_Cultural_Encounters_in_Late_Antiquity_and_the_Early_Middle_Ages_v_37_93_110) — early-sixth-century growth to approximately 500k, Egyptian grain-import system and migration from many provinces. - [Koç University Byzantine Constantinople history guide](https://libguides.ku.edu.tr/byzantineconstantinople/historyofconstantinople) — maximum population estimates range widely from 250k to one million, cautioning against making a top-end speculative figure firm. - [Urban Development in China (Cambridge Journal of Regions, Economy and Society)](https://academic.oup.com/cjres/article/9/3/467/2402972) — valuable counterexample estimating Song Kaifeng around 400k circa 1000–1100, demonstrating significant methodological uncertainty. Applications to Eryndor rather than population corrections: 1. Big cities have specialized civic services: fire brigades, port inspectors, caravan brokers, public clinics, aid granaries, sanitation officers, night watches and street-repair crews; the particulars vary by kingdom and era. The precedent that Song China operated fire stations and public welfare is a stronger inspiration than portraying all medieval people as living without such institutions. 2. Busy markets really are plausible: Kaifeng's elaborate shopfronts, restaurants, markets and street traffic inspire mixed-species market districts, Guild Street, artisans and festive life. Different-size residents in Eryndor create striking architectural accommodations. 3. Administration matters: Constantinople's state-controlled grain rations and formal capital rights; Cairo's dense bazaars, property law and tax regimes; China's canals, cargo commerce and well-developed urban organizations give diverse models. Blend influences without copying a specific culture wholesale. 4. Ancient cities can endure, evolve and collapse: A thousands-year-old civilization can develop spectacular municipal institutions but also face plague, civil disorder, financial shocks, severe dynastic change and urban decline. City size does not prove every reign or institution remained unchanged for millennia. 5. Respect historical uncertainty: Differences of urban core versus metropolitan area, household counts versus head counts, and different centuries affect every estimate. Do not cite old high-end guesses as if confirmed, nor treat estimates as worldbuilding restrictions. Provenance: This is an added researched comparison in response to the owner mentioning Constantinople, Cairo and large ancient Chinese cities. Existing Eryndor places and demographics remain untouched, no in-world research has been completed by Gloin and no game time has advanced. ## Fantasy-scale demographics and consequences of mass upheaval — creator priority Explicit creator clarification: Eryndor's population and settlement scales should be larger and more ambitious than ordinary historical comparisons. The world contains long-established civilizations, immense cities, powerful armies, terrifying monsters, advanced and wondrous technologies, and magical phenomena. Great population centers make it possible for war, invasion, disease, siege, mass enslavement, ecological disasters and magical catastrophes to cause enormous losses of life, potentially reaching hundreds of thousands or more in an extreme regional or continental crisis. These possibilities are stakes, not preset body counts. Birth-rate freeze — explicit creator instruction: Do not alter, increase, accelerate or invent birth/fertility rates to justify large populations or to replace catastrophic losses. Preserve every already established species- and region-specific reproduction pattern. Where no numerical birth rate was previously set, leave it unquantified rather than guessing one. Long historical timescales, immigration, existing settlement patterns and fantasy-world scale can coexist with unchanged births; any post-catastrophe recovery takes real in-world time and may never fully occur. Larger possible casualty totals do not imply faster births. - Don't shrink existing numbers: Legacy historical context: Karak-Varn was then modeled at 3.8 million, with the older Khazari, Eldar and Urakai totals unchanged at that stage; those figures were later superseded by the adopted sixfold world census (current Karak-Varn 22.8 million). The new 343.8m atlas-wide numerical model is a provisional simulation baseline, not a cap on what fantasy-scale Eryndor may contain. Other populations can be revised or expanded at the owner's direction and as new regions are developed; do not invent a population revision now merely to support a hypothetical casualty. - Large losses have persistent aftermath: Count soldiers and civilians separately where possible. Missing people, prisoners, refugees, destroyed households, abandoned hamlets, orphaned children, injured survivors, displaced artisans, food shortages, changing tax bases and intergenerational resentment can reshape a realm. Historical institutions provide inspiration for recovery, relief, rebuilding, conscription and labor migration, but cannot prohibit extraordinary fantasy events. - Not every battle kills millions: An army may retreat, a siege may lift, a catastrophe may be prevented, an epidemic may be contained. Losses and outcomes depend on the actual scale, exposure, threats, preparation, decisions, magic and defenses. Avoid exaggerating ordinary skirmishes or making devastation inevitable just to prove Eryndor is grimdark. - Demographics change over time: If destruction actually occurs during play, update the affected region's residents, refugee flows, farming labor, reconstruction, military strength, inheritance and diplomacy. A civilization can have existed for millennia while enduring expansions, disasters, migrations and recovery rather than continuous unbroken growth. - Campaign safeguard: These are possible future consequences, not a claim that an unseen mass-casualty event has already happened. The world does not advance during the current Day 22 11:25 AM pause, and Gloin knows only what he could learn in-world. ## Regional cultures and subcultures — new complete living-culture expansion Explicit creator rule: Every intelligent people has multiple cultures; every region contains overlapping local subcultures. The distinctive Khazari idea that contribution earns respect is not a generic value imposed on Eldar, Urakai, Halflings, Centaurs, Merfolk, Goblins or other peoples. Each community has its own admired paths, kinship traditions, duties, taboos and dissenting individuals. Culture comes from species + continent + settlement + state + occupation + household + life experience, and shared multi-species village identity can override older labels. 1. Some Khazari are legendary masters who also raise substantial families. Others live with partners and children while being perfectly competent, ordinary craftspeople without pursuing perfection. Others devote centuries to becoming masters and never form a family. Some do not choose mastery but still do honest work, maintain friendships and households, and contribute to their communities. Being unmarried, childless, married, highly skilled or unexceptional in one's trade is not itself grounds for stigma. The real cultural expectation is useful effort: A Khazari who is capable of contributing yet deliberately chooses permanent idleness and expects others to carry their burden may face disapproval, gossip and loss of respect. Dwarven culture values work, effort, service, responsibility and craft, not just extraordinary talent. A reliable journeyman, farmer, trader, clerk, cook or parent can be respected alongside a master engineer. Apprenticeship, study, running a household, raising children, caring for relatives, public service and community duties count as meaningful work; contributing need not mean wage employment or physically strenuous labour. Fairness and individual variety: Illness, disability, injury, involuntary unemployment, bereavement, age, recovery and genuine difficulty finding work are not equivalent to choosing laziness. Different Khazari individuals and clans may judge people more harshly or more generously, and a town can have internal debates about inherited wealth, early retirement or what counts as service. These are social expectations, not compulsory species instincts or a universal criminal law. Long lives and demographics: Overlapping generations and large extended families remain integral to Eryndor. Mastery and family may coexist for centuries. No birth rates, fertility biology, populations, marriage ratios or character ages change. Tolkien's isolated or unmarried craft-absorbed Dwarves are one possible archetype, not a general rule imposed on the Khazari. Gloin-specific continuity: Gloin Hammerfeld, 42, is recorded as not employed and not enlisted at the Day 19 opening, but he is actively pursuing work, instruction, research and a direction in life. Do not narrate that his family or society has branded him lazy merely because his employment status was unset; reactions require dialogue and actual behaviour in play. His family Durgan, Mara, Bruni, Tovin and Elska remains unchanged. ## Creator correction — ancient lives AND large family networks Despite centuries-long hobbies, crafts and scholarship, Eryndor's Khazari, Eldar and other long-lived peoples still have the large extended family dynamics already established, including overlapping generations, siblings, parents and clans. The Hammerfeld household remains Durgan, Mara and four children (Bruni, Gloin, Tovin, Elska). The Tolkien comparison must not be reinterpreted as mandatory small families or celibacy. No birth rate or reproduction assumptions change. Different individuals still pursue romance, marriage, family, service, scholarship, making, adventure and politics in different balances; a changed focus does not mean every Elf is selfish. Preserve all existing birth rates and populations without alteration. See 02 — Peoples & Cultures for examples and source separation. ## Governing creative direction — rule of cool before historical realism Final creator clarification: Looking ridiculous is neither proof of failure nor proof of success. A fantastical device, unconventional plan or impossible-looking stunt is evaluated on what actually happens in Eryndor—skill, circumstance, capability, preparation and resistance—not its appearance or mundane Earth's plausibility. Rule of Cool permits extraordinary outcomes but does not grant automatic success. The 40K Orks were a joke/reference point, not literally imported mechanics. See the Campaign Rules' explicit statement of this distinction. Use real historical records to enrich grounded society—trade, law, agriculture, workplaces, guilds, slavery, military organisation, medicine, culture—not to police the fantasy's geography, gravity, moons, magic, technology spectacle or established population scale. Karak-Varn now stands at 22.8 million in the current model; the old 3.8-million baseline is retained only for historical comparison. The creator's established story, character agency and pause remain binding. See 10 — Campaign Rules & Play Systems. ## Grimdark world layer — slavery and conflict without species determinism At the owner's direction, Eryndor includes real enslavers, captive raiders, debt bondage, coerced labor and kingdoms or officials that profit from these practices. The creator further clarifies that any intelligent people can enslave its own members or members of another people, for a multitude of motives. A hypothetical Urakai warlord capturing Khazari miners is one example and must not be made the central default or silently identified with a prior unnamed warlord. See Eryndor Living Atlas VII — Slavery, Bondage, Serfdom & Resistance for jurisdictional variation, factions, motives, resistance, and source status. This is new, revisable worldbuilding, not a retroactive Day 19–22 event. ## Patchwork-town danger correction — creator's explicit instruction The same patchwork-town atmosphere must not make Eryndor safe or sanitized. The creator specifically wants it possible for a powerful, previously welcome resident such as an Ogre to commit a deadly rampage, forcing ordinary townsfolk and guards to stop them, perhaps fatally. Such an attack, if it occurs during actual gameplay time, is dangerous and produces real deaths, injuries, consequences and investigation. It is not established that any named individual will do this, nor that violence is innate to a species. Eryndor Living Atlas VI — Patchwork Villages & Folktale Crossroads now states this rule explicitly; player choice and normal in-world causality govern events. ## Patchwork towns and fairy-tale crossroads — creator's preferred social atmosphere The owner clarified that some settlements should resemble lively multi-species folktale communities: Pigfolk, Wolvenkin, Foxfolk, Goblins, Gnomes, Brownies, Pixies, Trolls, Ogres, Satyrs and other established sapient peoples sharing streets, stores and neighbourly feuds. Gloin has not left Karak-Varn: the campaign remains paused at Day 22, 11:25 AM at Hadrik's desk, awaiting the player's response; future travel options do not imply an accepted quest. ## Purpose and organisation This edition is a comprehensive, expandable reference for the fantasy world of Eryndor and the continuing campaign of Gloin Hammerfeld. Direct creator decision, including explicit revisions to established lore, takes priority for the current canon, while the superseded version remains part of the change history. 2. Established in play or established reference canon: confirmed in-world events and adopted world facts, subject to later creator revision. 3. Reported: an NPC's statement, rumour, witness account, incomplete archival account or political report; the report's existence is canon, but its claim may be false or incomplete. 4. Hypothesis / interpretation: reasoned possibilities from Gloin, Maela, Borin, Hadrik or others. A hypothesis is not a revealed answer. 5. Disputed / contradictory source: source texts disagree. Record both positions and avoid choosing silently; use explicit creator direction or verified later chronology to settle. 6. Unknown / deliberately open: no established answer. Do not decide an unseen truth in advance. 7. Proposed: unused future-development suggestion, not canon until accepted. All canon is revisable. This does not mean all present facts are equally uncertain: adopted canon remains the working reality until explicitly changed. Prior drafts, rumours, tentative future concepts and NPC conjectures are not automatically binding. ## Absolute roleplay invariants - Gloin Hammerfeld is the player character. The player alone decides his dialogue, actions, inner thoughts, choices, friendships, fighting style and personal future. Never write those choices on his behalf. - His ancestry and any potential connection with the First Throne remain genuinely unknown, with no predetermined secret reveal or chosen-one premise. Direct descent is possible in principle, not established. - NPCs have independent lives, motives, loyalties, fallible knowledge and social histories. Do not make all NPCs privy to the same discoveries; track who actually heard what. - Do not advance the world clock, research, offscreen incidents or NPC actions while the campaign is paused. When play resumes, advance only as actions and reasonable passage of in-world time require. - No guaranteed plot armour or conveniently predetermined resolution; earned skills, costs, consequences and uncertain evidence all matter. - End every active roleplay response with three to five numbered optional suggestions for Gloin's next dialogue or action, without treating any suggestion as his actual choice. - Do not treat any people as innately evil or virtuous. Local dangerous reputations and exceptionally rare benevolent exceptions can coexist with culturally rich, varied people. - Do not infer that all ruins, ancient machines, lunar anomalies, magical theories or disappearances relate to the First Throne. ## Sixfold world census is now the current baseline — 21 November 2026 Population resimulation completed: The creator explicitly accepted a 6× revision of previously simulated Year 3847 populations. Gloin's Year 3847, Era of Crowns, Fifth Age campaign remains paused at Hadrik's desk, Autumn Day 22 \~11:25 AM. ## Creator directive — expanded village network, minor cities and 5–7× capital scale Creator's latest demographic direction (21 November 2026; accepted worldbuilding direction, exact totals pending): In the substantially enlarged 50,000-km Eryndor, particularly Avarra, the absolute number of rural inhabitants and scattered villages should rise dramatically. The Veiled Inland Sea's connected but outside-isolated shore villages remain separately governed by the established concealment premise. ## Peoples' distinct magical traditions survive the expanded cosmology (creator clarification, 21 November 2026) Binding distinction: The creator explicitly retains the different kinds of magic long associated with Khazari (dwarves), Eldar (elves), Aelwyn Fae, fairy peoples such as Pixies, Gnomes, and other peoples. These are legitimate distinct cultural, practical, possibly innate or supernatural traditions in the setting, not merely interchangeable labels for generic lunar spells. A tradition may have customary methods, ethics, rites, materials, aptitudes and histories, but the detailed disciplines and mechanisms outside already defined Khazari examples remain to be developed—not manufactured retrospectively. Do not merge Aelwyn Fae with Pixies/fairy folk, or make Gnome magic a copy of Khazari rune systems. Individual members of any people are not required to practise any tradition; cross-cultural learning and overlapping magic are possible when consistent with training and ability. Exact already-established Khazari traditions: Runecraft (symbols and enchantments); Deepcraft (stone, earth and subterranean perception/workings); Forgebinding (magical craft and durability); Hearthmagic (warmth, preservation, protection and domestic/settlement uses); Stonecalling (rare mountain-sense/communication); Ancestral Binding (controversial bloodline, oath and hereditary work). Keep them individually distinct, not automatically all lunar or inherently benevolent. Established broad fields include Arcana, Nature, Divination, Bloodcraft, Runecraft and Shadowcraft; these are not exhaustive nor species-exclusive. Moral aspect: Some magical forces are inherently good, some morally grey and some inherently evil, regardless of the caster's intentions. Do not assign an inherent moral alignment to an entire people, civilization, cultural school or broad discipline without specific creator definition; a tradition can contain different techniques and moral natures. This distinction adds nuance to the system without erasing Fae, fairy, Gnome, Eldar, Khazari or other magical heritage. Cosmic sources and knowledge: Moons are literal sources of lunar magic and people know that fact, but not how/why or which moon creates which magical force; some moons show almost no effects, others much stronger.
